opus-5.5.text:
I think there are really three or four objectives that have to be satisfied at the same time, and that's what makes it hard.

The first and most obvious one is identity preservation. If you're asking for a picture of specific people, each person has to actually look like themselves: their facial structure, their skin tone, their hairstyle, the subtle features that make them recognizable. And it has to hold up across different poses, expressions, and lighting conditions, not just a frontal headshot. People are very sensitive to faces. If something is slightly off, you notice immediately.

The second is what I'd call identity disentanglement, or avoiding identity leakage. Once you have multiple people in the same image, the model tends to blend them. Features from one person bleed into another, or two people end up looking like siblings when they're not. So the system has to keep each identity separate and bind it to the right person in the scene. That's a binding problem, and diffusion models aren't naturally good at it, because attention mixes everything together.

The third objective is compositional and prompt fidelity. The user usually wants more than just faces. They describe a setting, a layout, an activity: "the four of us at the beach, two sitting, two standing." The model has to respect that layout, the number of people, their relative positions, the interactions between them, while still keeping each identity intact. There's a real tension here. The more strongly you enforce identity, the more you tend to constrain pose and composition, and the image starts to look like faces pasted onto a scene.

Which brings me to the fourth: overall realism and coherence. The group has to look like it was actually captured together. Consistent lighting, consistent scale and perspective, natural occlusions when people overlap, plausible body proportions. And the people should look like they're interacting with each other and the environment, not standing in isolation.

On top of those, from a practical standpoint, you'd like it to work efficiently, ideally without fine-tuning a separate model for every person, maybe from just one or a few reference images. And you want it to generalize to arbitrary numbers of people.

So the core challenge is balancing these. Each one individually is somewhat solved, but satisfying identity, separation, composition, and realism all at once in a single image is where the interesting research is.

r001.rationale: The response identifies identity preservation as an objective: each depicted person must look like themselves, and it notes that the system may use one or a few reference images.

r002.rationale: The response discusses poses, expressions, and composition, but does not identify having the people look at the camera as an objective.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure, that's a great question, and it's actually one that really exposes the limits of current generation models. When you think about it, a group picture of specific people is a much harder problem than generating a single face, because you're layering several objectives that tend to compete with each other.

The first and most obvious one is identity preservation. If I give the system a few reference photos of, say, five different people, each of those people has to come out looking like themselves, not like some averaged or blended version. And this is where most systems break down. The moment you have more than one or two subjects, you get what we call identity leakage or identity mixing, where features from one person bleed into another. Person A ends up with person B's nose, or the hair color drifts. So you need some mechanism, whether it's in the attention layers or in how you condition the model, that keeps each identity bound to its own region and its own subject.

The second objective is composition and layout. In a real group photo, people have spatial relationships. Someone is in front, someone is behind, they're standing at plausible scales relative to each other, they're occluding each other in realistic ways. The model has to understand that these are separate entities occupying a shared 3D space and not just paste faces onto a canvas. And you often want some control over that, where the user can say "put this person on the left, this one in the middle."

Third, there's the question of interaction and coherence. If it's supposed to look like a group picture, the lighting has to be consistent across everyone. The camera perspective has to be consistent. If the scene is outdoors at sunset, everyone should be lit by the same sunset. That sounds trivial but when you're composing from independent references, each of which was taken under different conditions, harmonizing all of that is actually quite difficult.

Then fourth, you still need to follow the text prompt. People want to say "these five people at a beach, wearing casual clothes, laughing." So the identity conditioning cannot be so strong that it overrides the semantics of the prompt. There's a real tension there. If you push identity fidelity too hard, you end up basically copying the reference photos, same pose, same expression, same clothing. If you push prompt adherence too hard, you lose the identities. Finding the right balance is probably the central engineering problem.

And I'd add a fifth one, which is more practical: it should be efficient and it should not require per-subject fine-tuning. The early approaches like DreamBooth-style methods needed you to train a model for each person, and that simply doesn't scale to a group of five or ten people. So you want a feed-forward, encoder-based approach where you can inject the identities at inference time.

So to summarize, I'd say identity preservation per subject without mixing, controllable spatial layout, global scene consistency, prompt adherence, and doing all of it without test-time training. Getting all five simultaneously is really where the research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says each person should look like themselves based on supplied reference photos and emphasizes preserving each identity without blending.

r002.rationale: The response discusses layout, perspective, and prompt-controlled poses, but does not identify having the people look at the camera as an objective.

astra-6.text:
I think there are several objectives that have to be satisfied together. First is identity: each person should actually look like the person you asked for. A realistic face is not enough if it’s the wrong face. And when you have multiple people, you need to preserve those identities independently, without mixing their features or duplicating someone.

Then there is following the description. Are all the requested people present? Are they in the right positions, wearing the requested clothing, and interacting in the way you intended? Finally, the image needs to be coherent as a whole—the lighting, perspective, proportions, and occlusions should make sense, so it feels like these people were photographed together.

The challenge is satisfying all of those at once. You can produce a beautiful group picture and still fail because one person is missing or someone’s identity has changed.

r001.rationale: It says each person should look like the person requested and that identities must be preserved independently, which communicates matching generated faces to the supplied references.

r002.rationale: The response discusses positions, clothing, interactions, and overall coherence, but does not mention having the people look at the camera.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are several objectives that have to be satisfied together. First is identity: if you ask for a picture of specific people, each person should actually look like themselves. It is not enough to generate a plausible group of faces. And those identities should remain distinct, without mixing one person’s features into another’s.

Second is following the description—who is in the picture, where they are, what they are doing, and how they relate to one another. If you ask for three people, you should get those three people, with the right attributes assigned to each.

Then there is the quality of the image as a whole. The lighting, perspective, scale, and interactions should be coherent, so it looks like these people were photographed together. The challenge is satisfying all of those objectives simultaneously: preserving each identity while still giving the model enough freedom to create a natural composition.
